## d281: affection, desire

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d281 |
| Comparative input | *aẓ-i-; *aẓ(i)-k-ar- and *aẓ-ti formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ẓ / singleton |
| Following vowel | i |
| Root/formation shape | VC-i-C / VC-C |
| Grammatical category | noun/verb |
| Boundary evidence | i-stem and consonantal extensions independently attested; exact historical age of -kar unknown. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Malayalam aṛ̆ivu and Kannada aṛ̆ipu independently support vowel-first *aẓi; Kannada aṛ̆kaṟ beside akkaṟe directly supplies the relevant medial-cluster comparison.

**Direction.** Kannada preserves both ẓk and kk, favoring assimilation after medial syncope. Telugu akkaṟa remains vowel-initial, so its missing ẓ does not require an earlier initial promotion.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aẓi-kar > *aẓkar > akkar gives Telugu akkaṟa and Kannada akkaṟe with regressive assimilation ẓk>kk. *aẓ-ti > arti retains the rhotic-order reflex in another formation; remaining suffix vowels vary independently.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** DEDR tentatively relates burn/grieve d276, so root independence needs a sensitivity collapse. Tulu arti has an alternative long-root d381 comparison. Toda arkyn and Kota akm have different final morphology; their exact full derivations are less secure than the initial-order diagnosis.

**Mechanism scope.** Medial syncope and regressive consonant assimilation, not initial apical displacement

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 281 and cross-references d276,381

<a id="d282"></a>
## d282: cry, weep, call

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d282 |
| Comparative input | *aẓ-u- / *aẓ-ay-; regional vowel history unresolved |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ẓ / singleton |
| Following vowel | u/a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-V / VC-V-C |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | u/ay and causative formations independently attested; exact formative vowels for short Pengo and long Kui stems not forced. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṛ̆u/aṛ̆ai, Malayalam aṛ̆uka, Kannada aṛ̆u and Gondi–Konda aṛ- independently establish vowel-first apical and at least u/ay formations. PSS83 pp.14–15 compares *aẓ-u; the database Starostin *jeẓ head is an alternative analysis, not adopted as a given.

**Direction.** Agreement of SD I, Gondi–Konda, Central Dravidian and retained Pengo aṛ- favors earlier V–ẓ. Kui/Kuvi/Manda initial ṛ are innovative under this cognacy, but their ī needs a regional vowel explanation. Pengo causatives supply a within-language original/displaced contrast.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Retained *aẓ-u > Telugu ēḍu- requires vowel fronting/lengthening before or alongside ẓ>ḍ; ēḍucu has an incorporated past palatal according to K03 p.193. Pengo aṛ-/aṛba versus ṛat/ṛatpa shows apical displacement in causative formations; a possible *aẓ-a-t > ṛat route remains conditional. Kui/Kuvi/Manda *aẓV > ṛī is directionally plausible, but a uniquely supported sequence yielding ī is not yet available.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Telugu long ē does not mean metathesis: the apical is still after the vowel. Pengo ṛatpa is a source correction of earlier aratpa, which would reverse its outcome classification if not followed. Tulu leppuni/leppu/lāvu may involve local aphaeresis/contraction or another root; DEN1 corrects lāvu for earlier levu. Badaga aḷu/avu/au exemplifies lateral lenition/loss. Gondi R Epic aḍusānā could reflect contact and is not needed to establish native retention.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 282; DEN1 1972 p.400 entry 240; PSS83 pp.14–15; K03 p.193

## d285: dip, press, immerse

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d285 |
| Comparative input | *aẓ-unt- / *aẓ-utt- |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ẓ / singleton |
| Following vowel | u |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṛ̆untu/aṛ̆uttu and Malayalam aṛ̆untuka/aṛ̆uttuka independently support high u and transitivity-related dental extensions. Kannada aṛ̆du beside addu preserves an intermediate medial cluster.

**Direction.** Southern high-vowel stems and retained Kannada ẓd provide a direct route to Telugu dd by medial syncope and assimilation. No language in the reviewed set requires initial apical movement.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aẓ-unt/utt > *aẓd > addu in Telugu/Kannada; Kannada ajju and Kota aj require an additional local palatal-cluster development. Tulu arduni retains a rhotic-plus-stop cluster. The details of dental voicing/strengthening are conditional, but initial-vowel deletion is unnecessary.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** DEDR’s possible link to long-root d396 āẓ could change the remote root quantity; retain that as a sensitivity issue rather than assign long input from an uncertain cross-reference. Gadaba addap blot closely resembles Telugu addu and could be a loan; donor evidence is not explicit, so do not count it as independent phonological confirmation.

**Mechanism scope.** Medial syncope and cluster assimilation; independent palatal outcomes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 285 and tentative cross-reference 396

## d291: strength, size, ability

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d291+d295 |

| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aḷ strength and Kannada aḷa/aḷavu/aḷavi support short a and postvocalic lateral independently. Telugu alavi/alavu retain exactly the kind of low-vowel expansion compared in measure d295.

**Direction.** Independent southern vowel-first forms and Konda alvi favor *aḷav > lāv. The long Konda āl is a retained-order quantity variant, not evidence of an original initial lā-.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aḷ-av > *ḷāv > Telugu lāvu, alongside retained alavi/alavu. Gondi lāv, Kolami la·v and Parji lāv could reflect the same historical development or spread of the Telugu adjective/noun; local donor diagnostics are needed.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Treat d291 and d295 as one conservative root family: Kannada/Telugu repeat alavi/alavu and lāvu with overlapping size, power and capacity meanings. This does not assert that every measurement-verb suffix was already part of one undifferentiated proto-lexeme. DEDR’s comparison with long-root d399 is tentative and should be tested as a quantity alternative. Konda lāvu much resembles the Telugu broad adjective and may be borrowed.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 291,295; tentative cross-reference 399

## d295: measure, size

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d291+d295 |
| Comparative input | *aḷ-a-; *aḷ-a-p/-v and dental extensions |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ḷ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-C |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Low a and labial/dental derivative alternations corroborated independently in SD I. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | high |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aḷa/aḷavu/aḷappu, Kannada aḷe/aḷavu and Kodagu aḷa independently support low a and postvocalic lateral. Telugu alavi supplies a retained related measure noun.

**Direction.** SD I and retained Telugu alavi support earlier *aḷav rather than initial *lāv with repeated prothesis. Kui/Kuvi/Pengo initial apical forms are therefore innovations under the shared measurement comparison.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aḷ-av > *ḷāv > lāvu in Telugu, with separate ḷ>l. Related palatal extensions give Kuvi/Pengo lāc and Kui ḍās/ḍāc, requiring local lateral-to-stop correspondence. Tulu aḷapuni > lappuni is compatible with aphaeresis and strengthening; K03 p.117 explicitly groups its short-vowel counterpart under aphaeresis.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Telugu alavi and lāvu are not independent roots. Tulu short lapp- should not be equated uncritically with Telugu long lāv-. Manda lēc has unexplained e, so quantity/quality tests exclude it pending a supported vowel history. Badaga ādu measured has an explicitly cited archaic aldu precursor, evidence for lateral loss plus contraction/lengthening, not promotion. Toda’s Q in the DEDR digital tense string is a transcription issue; retain raw data and use independent Toda citation for order.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 295; K03 p.117; Hockings & Pilot-Raichoor 1992 pp.4,38,43 (citing Emeneau 1939 p.46)

## d296: mix, join, approach, seize

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d296 |
| Comparative input | *aḷ-a- / *aḷ-ay-; *aḷ-p-? and other formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ḷ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-ay / VC-a-C / VC-C |
| Grammatical category | verb |
| Boundary evidence | -ay and low-vowel labial formations independently visible; exact consonantal Konda/Pengo formative remains uncertain. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aḷai/aḷa/aḷavu and Malayalam aḷayuka independently support low a and lateral after the vowel. Kannada aḷa/aḷavu agree; Telugu alamu has a different labial extension from lāyu.

**Direction.** The southern comparison and retained Telugu alamu favor V–ḷ. Initial l in Telugu lāyu and Konda/Pengo lap is innovative, but their different final formations prevent a single inferred vowel-quantity derivation.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aḷ-ay > *ḷāy > Telugu lāyu, with lateral merger; *aḷ-am > alamu retains order. Konda/Pengo *aḷ-p > lap/lab is one possible consonantal-formation displacement route; deriving them by shortening earlier *lāp requires independent evidence. Brahui halling retains a before l after initial h addition; h is not evidence for loss of the root vowel.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Mix/measure d295 share similar shapes but are not merged just because their roots are homophonous. Brahui ha in and hatining are associated morphological comparisons in the source; they are not independently counted as three reflexes of this root. Exact origin of Brahui h and stem grades requires its local grammar. Konda/Pengo short vowels may test formative conditioning once their earlier suffix is recovered.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 296; Brahui comparison cites Emeneau 1962 p.63

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aḷakam and Kannada aḷaka/aḷḷaka support an initial vowel and lateral; the Telugu nasal correspondence is explicitly queried by DEDR.

**Direction.** Under the cognacy, earlier V–ḷ is supported independently of Telugu. Telugu anuku remains vowel-first and therefore supplies no positive evidence of initial metathesis.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** DEDR suggests *aḷuku > *aṇuku > anuku, with lateral nasalization and loss of retroflexion. This is a conditional consonant-correspondence proposal; no unambiguous environment for ḷ>ṇ is established in this entry.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Do not count the proposed nasal route as regular until other independently cognate cases establish its conditioning. Difference a/u in the second vowel and liquid-state semantics could reflect a genuine formation alternation or questionable cognacy; additional regional fluid adjectives would discriminate.

## d299: saltpan, salt marsh

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aḷam/uppaḷam and Malayalam aḷam/upp-aḷam independently attest the free base and salt compound. Telugu attests only upp-aḷamu in this group.

**Direction.** Comparative free southern forms establish V–ḷ order of the second compound member. The Telugu compound does not itself supply a word-initial aḷ input at the time of sound change.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *uppu + aḷam > upp-aḷamu retains the vowel–lateral sequence within a compound. A borrowed whole compound would give the same attested result; the Telugu retroflex lateral merits a source/history check.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Exclude this from the decisive word-initial sound-law denominator unless the free base or date of composition can be established in Telugu. The compound is nevertheless a relevant boundary control. Native inheritance, preserved compound allomorph and borrowing remain alternatives; no loan is asserted merely from the ḷ spelling.

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aḷi and Malayalam aḷi/aḷikkuka independently establish high i; Kannada aḷipu/aḷupu supports related high-vowel labial formations. Telugu lā̃cu has a distinct nasal-palatal extension.

**Direction.** Agreement of Tamil, Malayalam and Kannada favors earlier aḷi-. Telugu initial l is plausibly displaced, but neither its long ā nor the nasal-palatal suffix may be used to invent a low formative in the input.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *aḷ-i-NC > *ḷaNC > lā̃cu would require later nasal loss with compensatory lengthening or a different independently reconstructed extension. A direct a+i > ā contraction conflicts with the short-vowel branch of K03 Rule 20. Without a matching derivative, the exact quantity history is unresolved.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** This is a candidate counterexample to an unrestricted prediction of short output after high-i input, not grounds for quietly changing i to a. Kota ayḷ mog twin children is semantically indirect; its glide/lateral order and relationship to unlinked ayḷ classificatory brother-in-law (f_cynufhnk3o6sm) need separate checking. The DEDR parse ayḷ with gloss mog twin children truncates the expression; Wolf’s source preserves the whole expression.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 301; Wolf Kota p.4 entry 3; compare K03 p.157 Rule 20

Telugu aḷuku = aluku is an editorial equivalence string, not a third lexical root.

**Direction.** The southern vowel-first base supports innovative initial l in Telugu, but the exact velar formation is not recovered solely from Telugu. Kurux lātā has different final morphology from alap and cannot automatically be called the same metathesis.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *aḷ-aŋk > *ḷāŋk > Telugu lā̃ga requires an unattested but morphologically plausible velar extension; *aḷay plus a later noun suffix is an alternative. Kurux alap > lātā cannot follow by initial a loss alone because p/t differs. Badaga ae can follow lateral loss in *aḷay without initial promotion.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** PSS83 p.56 example63 proposes moving Toda oḷb to the concealment family (old DED853, current d1015), because a before ay should not yield Toda o. That objection depends on comparing the identical ay formation; an independently justified different labial derivative could weaken it. Keep Toda cognacy ambiguous. The Kurub. aḷe source is mislabeled Malayalam and its precise lect is unresolved; neither it nor the parsed heading is counted as Malayalam evidence.

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟaŋ-kai, Telugu aṟa-cēyi/aṟa-kālu and Kolami ārankei/árungkei independently attest an aṟ/an-bearing first component in body-part compounds. Its precise sense and nasal segmentation are unresolved.

**Direction.** All source forms retain a vowel before the apical. These are initial compound members, so the compound boundary is after the candidate sequence rather than before it as in saltpan d299.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṟa(n)+kai gives the compared palm compounds, with hand replaced by Telugu cēyi and foot kālu in parallel formations. Kolami length and n/ŋ variants have separate source histories; no initial apical displacement occurs.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** The source explicitly says ārankei has n, not ŋ. The parser split that editorial correction into fragments, including a spurious standalone ŋ. Do not count the compound as a bare free root; equally, a following compound boundary alone cannot explain its retention, since anvil d86 changes in that position. Possible connection to half/inner/partition vocabulary needs independent semantic evidence.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 310 p.29 (DEDS(N) 42), original source checked

## d314: know, understand, inquire

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d314 |
| Comparative input | *aṯ-V-; regional *eṟ-uk/ŋk- |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṯ / singleton |
| Following vowel | unknown |
| Root/formation shape | VC-V / VC-V-C |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | i-root and distinct u/velar expansion visible; exact regional proto-vowel and age of extension unresolved. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core-formation-uncertain |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟi, Malayalam aṟiyuka, Kannada aṟi and the independent K03 *aṯ-V reconstruction support a vowel-first alveolar root. Telugu eṟũgu has a distinct high-u velar/nasal extension; rare Tamil aruku supports investigating that formation but has a different rhotic spelling.

**Direction.** Agreement of multiple southern languages and Brahui vowel-before-r favors V–alveolar order. Telugu eṟũgu is therefore a retained candidate, not a metathesized item concealed merely by initial e.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṯ-V > southern aṟi; regional *a/eṟ-uk/ŋk > Telugu eṟũgu/eṟuka retains initial order while vowel and formative changes occur. Kota *ar-y > ayr is a separate glide/apical transposition; Brahui harrifing has initial h while preserving vowel-before-r.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** PSS83 p.229 explicitly lists the Telugu know form among exceptions to generalized apical metathesis. Unknown age and vowel of its exact extended input limit a fully specified law test, but are not proof that it was ineligible. Kolami erka is explicitly a Telugu loan. Badaga aḷi search has an unexplained lateral beside ari/aru forms and is not normalized to r.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 314; PSS83 p.229; K03 reconstruction; Hockings & Pilot-Raichoor 1992 pp.28–29,38

## d315: sever, cut, decrease, scratch

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d315 |
| Comparative input | *aṯ-u- / *aṯ-al- and velar/labial formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṯ / singleton |
| Following vowel | u |
| Root/formation shape | VC-u-C / VC-a-C |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Independent high-u bare sever stem versus low-al and velar/labial expansions; no single extension assigned across all reflexes. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟu, Malayalam aṟuka and Kannada aṟu independently establish a high-u sever root; Tamil aṟal supplies a separate low-vowel detachment formation. Telugu aṟu retains the root, while ṟakku/rakku has a velar extension.

**Direction.** Broad southern vowel-first evidence and Brahui harring support earlier V–alveolar ordering. Telugu scratch ṟakku is innovative under this cognacy; the velar derivative’s exact vowel is not automatically identical to that of the bare sever stem.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṯ-u > Telugu aṟu; conditional *aṟ-uk(k) > *ṟakk > ṟakku/rakku gives short a after a different high vowel. Alternative consonantal *aṟ-kk formation yields the same output, so suffix-vowel identity is not uniquely recovered. Brahui harring adds h before the retained vowel-r sequence.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** K61 p.56’s proposed comparison for Telugu rālu invokes Tamil aṟal from this family, linking it to d233 as an alternative analysis. Do not count this source cross-family borrowing of evidence twice. Kolami/Naikri ark may instead belong to cut d175. DEDR also compares n-initial naṟukku d3625: initial n loss versus separate lexical roots needs testing. Badaga place/plant compounds and archaic harakada do not all have equally secure cognacy.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 315 p.29; K61 p.56; cross-references d175,233,3625

## d316: digest, wear away, indigestion

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d316 |
| Comparative input | *aṯ-u-; *aṟ-ak/uk- and labial formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṯ / singleton |
| Following vowel | u/a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-V-C |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Regional velar formation independently corroborated; other labial/nasal-palatal formations not forced into it. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟu digest and Kannada aragu/aṟave independently support vowel-first apical and different extensions. Telugu aṟugu, Konda aṟgi and Kuvi arg provide a directly comparable regional velar stem.

**Direction.** SD I and SD II agree on vowel-before-apical in the core digestion comparison. Tulu reñjuni and Gondi rokk are initial-r outliers whose vowels and extensions must be checked before accepting metathesis.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṟ-Vk > Telugu aṟugu, Konda aṟgi and Kuvi arg with regional vowel/syncope differences. Tulu arkame/akku supplies a plausible medial rk>kk route. Conditional *ar-Vñc > reñjuni would require initial loss/displacement plus a separately supported e history.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Original DEDR explicitly questions the Gondi rokkānā/rokk comparison; its o and kk cannot be explained by writing an invented earlier *oru solely to fit it. Kui ārgagāṭi giva is a full light-verb construction whose nominal component may have a contact history. The indigestion subentry has ṟ/ẓ variation and different nouns; do not treat every nasal/velar form as the same input.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 316(a,b) p.30, original question mark on Gondi checked

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟu and aṟuppu fort independently support the high-u base and labial formation; Telugu aṟupu is a keep/preserve verb. Tamil aṟai camp has a different low-vowel formation.

**Direction.** Both languages preserve a before the alveolar, supporting the compared regional input. No displaced form is attested in this group.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṟ-u-p > Telugu aṟupu; Tamil stronger *aṟ-u-pp > aṟuppu fort. Tamil aṟku/alku may reflect medial syncope and consonant variation but are explicitly questioned by the source.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** A two-language semantic bridge between dwell and preserve is plausible, not certain. A independently established early Telugu p-formation would strengthen its status as a counterexample to general metathesis; no such date is inferred just from modern retention. Do not explain it away as a free root: the Telugu form is visibly extended.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 317 p.30; Annamalai Tamil dictionary p.875 for aṟuppu

## d319: sound, shout, ring, prattle

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d319 |
| Comparative input | *aṯ-ay / *aṯ-a-; *-c/-p/-ŋk and consonantal extensions |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṯ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-C / VC-C |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Independent variation in formative vowels and consonants; K61 reconstructs rajju with consonantal extension. |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟai and Kannada aṟacu/aṟicu/aṟucu independently establish V–alveolar ordering and several extensions; Telugu aṟacu/aṟapu supply retained related forms. The exact input of rajju is less specific than the head *aṟ-a.

**Direction.** Multiple southern vowel-first forms favor earlier aṟ-. Telugu initial ṟ/r formations are innovative under the cognacy. Naiki arap and Gadaba arg support retained initial order outside SD I/Telugu.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** K61 p.55 compares rajju with consonantal *ar-j; Telugu ṟaŋke can reflect a nasal-velar derivative with displacement, while aṟacu/aṟapu retain order. Kui ṛaspa has a separate s/p cluster; its origin is not explained by simply adding -pa to modern Telugu. Kannada racce may reflect local displacement plus strengthening, but its cognacy/contact history remains unresolved.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Kannada racce was stranded in a gloss and would be missed by a search limited to Form; it is source-verified and added as one research observation. Gondi rāŋ(g) is explicitly queried by DEDR, so its long vowel does not automatically confirm a shared innovation. Kolami raz could be inherited or borrowed; no automatic Telugu loan is assumed. Koraga ajike lacks r and needs a local cluster-loss/cognacy explanation.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 319 p.30, original entry checked; K61 p.55 §1.130

## d321: rock, stone

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d321 |

| Initial consonant | Ø |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟai, Kannada aṟe and Kota ar independently support a vowel-first alveolar and an ay formation; Toda aṟ corroborates the consonant class. Telugu ṟāyi/rāyi preserves two rhotic spellings.

**Direction.** The shared SD I vowel-first forms favor *aṯ/ṟ-ay > ṟāy, not widespread insertion before an original *ṟāy. Kannada rāyi is explicitly borrowed from Telugu and cannot support an inherited Kannada innovation.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṟ-ay > *ṟāy > Telugu ṟāyi > rāyi, with later ṟ/r merger. Short ṟappa small stone has a different strong labial extension; *aṟ-pp > ṟapp is plausible, but shortening an earlier long vowel is not uniquely supported.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Badaga are is the lexical evidence; dozens of place names containing it are dependent derivatives and count as one family, with historical labels preserved. The precise *ṯ versus *ṟ reconstruction depends on the wider alveolar correspondence; modern Kannada is not assumed to preserve the proto manner of articulation.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 321; DEN1 1972 p.400 entry 271; Hockings & Pilot-Raichoor 1992 p.30

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṟai and Malayalam aṟa independently support singleton alveolar and ay formation; Telugu aṟa beside aṟṟa shows strengthening in a regional variant. Tulu adɛ has a stop reflex.

**Direction.** Shared vowel-first ordering supports older aṟay. Telugu singleton aṟa cannot be excluded from an eligible input class merely because the same entry also has a strengthened variant.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *aṟay > Tamil aṟai, Malayalam aṟa, Telugu aṟa; regional gemination yields Telugu aṟṟa and potentially Gondi arra. Tulu adɛ and Badaga -ādu require local alveolar/stop and quantity histories, without initial relocation.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** This is a near input match to displaced rock d321: a short initial vowel, singleton alveolar and ay noun. Different meanings do not create a phonological condition. Gondi arrā/arra could reflect Telugu contact; Muria ahpi has a substantially different cluster requiring an independent account. Badaga attests only compound components, so their word-boundary eligibility differs.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

## d328: fit, suitable, fertile

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d328 |
| Comparative input | *an-V-v-; possible older *can- comparison |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | n / singleton |
| Following vowel | u/a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-V-C |
| Grammatical category | adjective/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Regional labial derivative independently visible; possible older initial c is an unconfirmed deeper stage. |
| Input class | nasal-or-nasal-cluster-input |
| Telugu hypothesis | outside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule |
| Input confidence | medium |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | nasal-control |

**Independent input evidence.** Kannada anu/anavu/anuvu, Telugu anuvu and Kota anv support a nasal after the initial vowel and a labial extension. Tamil a/aṁ beauty is explicitly questioned; DEDR compares c-initial cannu d2423.

**Direction.** The regional vowel-first nasal input is supported independently of Telugu. A possible earlier initial c loss does not imply n has subsequently exchanged with a.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *an-V-v > Telugu anuvu and Kannada anavu/anuvu, Kota anv by medial syncope; Tulu anutana adds another nominal formative. No initial nasal displacement is observed.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Use as a nasal control, not as an automatic test of a rule restricted to nonnasal apicals. The Tamil loss/nasalization comparison and possible older c-bearing root need separate reconstruction. Vowel quality of the intervening syllable is variable rather than fixed from Telugu alone.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 328 p.30 and cross-reference 2423

<a id="d329"></a>
## d329: send, leave, start off

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d329 |
| Comparative input | *an-V-p-; high-u regional extension |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | a / short |
| C2 identity / structure | n / singleton |
| Following vowel | u |
| Root/formation shape | VC-u-p / VC-p |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Independent high-u stem and consonantal/labial variants; palatal and s-bearing derivatives kept distinct. |
| Input class | nasal-or-nasal-cluster-input |
| Telugu hypothesis | outside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | nasal-control |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil aṉuppu and Malayalam anuppuka independently establish high u and nasal before labial; Telugu anupu preserves the uncontracted order. Kannada ampaka, Kurux ambnā and Malto ambe support a consonantal nasal-labial variant.

**Direction.** Independent uncontracted southern forms plus Telugu anupu show that ampu need not reflect initial nasal metathesis: medial vowel deletion and place assimilation are sufficient.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *an-up > *anp > amp gives Telugu ampu and related labial-cluster forms; Telugu anucu/ancu needs a separate palatal extension or stem remodeling, not a p-to-c change assumed without context. Brahui hamp- adds initial h while preserving a before the nasal cluster.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** These are related derivatives and must count once per root. The relationship between full-vowel and consonantal formations could partly be inherited morphology rather than one universal syncope event. Gadaba anisp load on cart has an i/s extension whose history is not supplied by the basic send comparison.

**Mechanism scope.** Medial vowel loss and nasal place assimilation, no initial nasal displacement

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 329; Kobayashi 2022 reconstruction record *anVp-; Brahui source cites Emeneau 1962 p.63

<a id="d410"></a>
## d410: proximal demonstratives and adverbs

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | deictic-a-i |
| Comparative input | *i-t(u), *i-w-an/-ar; oblique *id-an-i / *iw-an-i, *iw-att-i |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short deictic input; secondary long formations |
| C2 identity / structure | t/w/b / morphological dental/labial elements |
| Following vowel | a/i/u/variable |
| Root/formation shape | deictic base + gender/number + oblique augment |
| Grammatical category | pronoun/adverb |
| Boundary evidence | Gender/number and oblique augments; proximal and distal members of one productive paradigm. |
| Input class | pronominal-morphology |
| Telugu hypothesis | outside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule |
| Input confidence | high for order; medium for immediate oblique prehistory |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | morphological-pronoun-domain |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil itu/ivaṉ, Malayalam itu/ivaṇ, Kannada idu/iva and Pengo/Manda idi/ivan establish initial i followed by gender/number material. The a- oblique augment is independently comparative in the matching distal paradigm (K03 p.222); the lexical source does not independently supply every uncontracted proximal oblique.

**Direction.** The a:i demonstrative opposition and the same following morphology across several branches support vowel-before-dental/labial input. Konda deni is particularly valuable because it does not simply copy the surface Telugu high vowel in dīni.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** K03 proposes lowering in *id-an-i > *ed-an-i before displacement/contraction, followed by Konda deni, while Telugu dīni is remodeled to preserve the opposition to interrogative dēni; this is analogy, not a phonetic i+a>ī rule. Compare *iw-an-i > Konda veni versus Telugu vīni, modern plural vīṭi from *iw-att-i with corresponding analogical possibilities. Konda ibe/ibeṇi : bēn/bēṇi supplies labial locative restructuring; Pengo ibe/ibṇi retains initial i even with syncope.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** The anti-homophony account for Telugu dīni is a plausible hypothesis (K03 p.223 n.14), not demonstrated by a directly attested earlier *deni stage. Sastri1969 pp.178,184 explicitly treats historical dēni as interrogative; an inscriptional English translation this grant is not sufficient to identify a proximal ancestral stage. Konda current DB plural oblique venka differs from K03 veni: preserve both source claims and do not silently replace morphology. Konda short deni versus long bēn shows formation-specific quantity. This cannot be used to validate a single phonetic outcome rule for all pronouns. Te nisuvu/nisũgu child is a separate semantic/cognacy issue within the giant deictic entry and is not evidence for nasal metathesis of the deictic base. Direct and oblique forms are research-split with links to their original unsplit database records.

**Mechanism scope.** Morphologically restricted displacement/contraction; Telugu high vowels plausibly analogical, not independent evidence for phonetic output.

**Scholarly references.** DEDR410; Krishnamurti2003 pp.158,222–223 nn.13–14

<a id="d432"></a>
## d432: split, crumble, crack

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d432 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-i- / *iṭ-a- and labial nominal extensions |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | i/a |
| Root/formation shape | VCV / VCVC |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | i/a verbal formations and u-p nominal formation independently attested; no single V2 assigned to all derivatives. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭi/iṭa, Malayalam iṭika/iṭakka, Kannada iḍi/iḍupu and Telugu iḍiyu/iḍupu support vowel-first order and more than one formative vowel independently.

**Direction.** Agreement on initial i before the apical across several branches favors earlier iṭ-, without assuming the Tamil forms alone are conservative.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭ-i > Telugu iḍiyu, Kannada iḍi; *iṭ-u-p > iḍupu in both. Kota/Toda lose final/medial vowels but retain the initial vowel. Irula ḍepisu may involve local aphaeresis after vowel lowering, but the source does not supply its immediate earlier form.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Irula is an uncertain local initial-loss candidate, not evidence that the Telugu innovation was shared with Irula. The nasal in iṇḍe needs a separate formation history. Pengo d2955 and Kolami d2974 are explicitly tentative comparisons and are not silently added to this root. Badaga idi is source-marked uncertain; do not treat hamlet Idukore as another root.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 432; cross-references 2955,2974 remain tentative

## d434: place, room, opportunity

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d434+d448 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-a-m / *iṭ-ay |
| Initial consonant | Ø |

| Following vowel | a |

| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭam/iṭai, Malayalam iṭam/eṭam and Kannada iḍe/eḍe agree on vowel-first i/e plus apical; Kota eṛm preserves the nominal m.

**Direction.** The shared vowel-first forms establish the pre-displacement order. Southern i/e alternation supports lowering before a, not a proto-initial d.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭ-am > *eḍam > Telugu eḍamu; *iṭ-ay > *eḍay > eḍa/eḍe. Kota and Toda shorten the word by final loss while keeping the first vowel. Tulu source contains dekki alongside iḍɛ, a likely local initial-loss formation with gemination.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Merge d434 with interval d448 for primary root counts: Tamil iṭai and Telugu eḍa/eḍamu recur with intersecting place/space senses. This avoids counting one spatial noun twice. The exact relationship of Tulu dekki to the other nominal formations remains unresolved and it is not automatically a SCDr-type contraction.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 434,448

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil/Malayalam iṭar, Kannada iḍaru/iḍuru and Old Telugu eḍaṟu support initial vowel plus apical. Tamil iṭumpai and Telugu iḍuma independently support a distinct labial/nasal derivative.

**Direction.** The historical Telugu retained form and southern comparison establish vowel-first ancestry. Telugu ḍepparamu is related semantically but its exact pp-bearing formation is not independently matched.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭ-ar > *eḍar > eḍaru; *iṭ-um(p) > iḍuma with independent labial changes. A conditional *iṭ-a-ppar > *ḍēppar > ḍeppar with pre-geminate shortening could yield ḍepparamu/depparamu, but the reconstructed extension is not established by iṭar alone.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Treat ḍepparamu as probable displacement with unresolved formation rather than inventing *-appar to guarantee the rule. eḍḍamu/eḍḍami have strengthening or cluster assimilation, not initial metathesis. The older obstruction verb may belong with stumble d437; that family collapse is a sensitivity, not an asserted etymology.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 435; tentative comparison 788

<a id="d437"></a>
## d437: stumble, hinder

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d437 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-aṟ / *iṭ-aŋk / *iṭ-Vp |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-C |
| Grammatical category | verb |
| Boundary evidence | Rhotic, nasal-velar and labial formations attested separately; exact Telugu strong velar suffix not assumed to be identical to all. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | medium |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil/Malayalam iṭaṟ-, Kannada iḍaṟu/eḍaṟu/eḍagu, Tulu eḍaŋkɯ and Malto iṛpe support initial vowel plus retroflex. The velar and rhotic extensions must be distinguished.

**Direction.** The comparative vowel-first order and Tulu dialect doublets establish earlier V–ṭ; Telugu ḍekku has shifted/lost the initial vowel under this cognacy.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *iṭ-a-k(k) > *eḍakk > *ḍēkk > ḍekku with shortening before kk. Tulu eḍaŋkɯ > ḍaŋkɯ/daŋkɯ is independently described as dialectal aphaeresis (K03 p.116), not a required same event. Kannada Havyaka ḍaŋku and Koraga ḍakki could be local losses or contact forms.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** The Telugu vowel e fits lowered *i before a, but its exact kk formation remains uncertain. Tulu dompu/dumpiyuni and doŋkɯ have labial/velar alternatives and rounded vowels that initial loss alone does not explain. Neither matching initial ḍ nor geographic proximity proves shared ancestry. Badaga erandu is source-uncertain and has an unexplained nasal sequence.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 437; DEN1 1972 p.400 entry 371; K03 p.116 citing Kekunnaya 1994 pp.42–44

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭi flour/confection and iṭiyappam, Malayalam iṭiyappam and Telugu iḍi/iḍikuḍumu agree on the vowel-first food base.

**Direction.** Independent southern food compounds corroborate vowel-first iṭi; there is no evidence here for a proto-initial ḍi.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭi > Telugu iḍi; appam/kuḍumu are separate compound components. The high-i match makes this a formal comparison to beat d443, but food-name diffusion may be later than the native change.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Possible relation to pounding/beat and to iṭṭali d455 must be considered in family sensitivity. Do not count each kind of cake as an independent negative. Culinary borrowing chronology is unresolved, so retain it as a lexical control rather than use it alone to falsify an inherited law.

<a id="d442"></a>
## d442: put, place, give

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d442 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-u- (past *iṭ-ṭ-); nominal *īṭ-u |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | u |
| Root/formation shape | VC-u / VC-C tense alternation |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Nonpast u and geminate past are independently supported; nominal length and causatives require formation-level classification. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭu : iṭṭ-, Kannada iḍu : iṭṭ-, Telugu iḍu, and matching Central Dravidian paradigms independently support high u and vowel-first root. Long īḍu nouns are a separate quantity formation.

**Direction.** Broad family distribution, including Kui/Kuvi/Pengo/Manda retention, supports original iṭ- order and rules out using Tulu dīpini as the reconstructive starting point.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭ-u > iḍu/ɨḍ-; past *iṭ-ṭ remains geminate in many languages. Gondi intervocalic ṭ corresponds to rhotic in ir/irr, Konda iṟ-, without initial relocation. Tulu dīpini beside iḍpini may show displacement, analogical remodeling or interaction with long īḍɯ; a literal *i+u contraction to ī is not established.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** The initial apical is singleton in the nonpast, despite past gemination; do not exclude the whole root as a geminate. Tulu dīḍɯ/jīḍɯ/ījɯ/īḍɯ require a linked paradigm/causative history, potentially d addition or expressive reinforcement; their shared ī is not evidence for a universal metathesis rule. Long nouns and aspectual auxiliary uses are not additional etyma.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 442; K03 Rule20 pp.157–158

<a id="d443"></a>
## d443: beat, strike, butt

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d443 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-i- / *iṭ-u- / *iṭ-a- formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | i |
| Root/formation shape | VC-i (beside u/a formations) |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | i-vocalism in the impact noun/verb is independently attested; do not replace all a/u extensions with i. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭi, Malayalam iṭi/iṭikka and Kannada iḍi independently support i+i, while Tamil iṭu and Kannada iḍaku support other formations. Kota/Toda, Kolami, Pengo and Kurux have vowel-first root cognates.

**Direction.** The independent high-i formation supports earlier iṭi > Telugu ḍī. Konda ṛey/ṛī were incorrectly assigned Kolami in the database: source p.43 makes Kolami iṛ- retained and Konda innovated.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭ-i > *ḍii > ḍī is a possible implementation of Rule20a; same-quality high vowels meet its contraction condition. Konda *iṭV > ṛī/ṛey involves its own apical correspondence and vowel variants. Kannada ḍī/ḍīku/ḍikki beside iḍi may be a Telugu loan, expressive reinforcement, or local displacement; no donor date yet decides.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Do not count Kannada and Telugu identical impact nouns automatically as independent changes. Telugu ḍīkonu is a light-verb/compound extension of ḍī, not another etymon. Imported Badaga sickle/iron-saw records have possible cut/iron segmentation rather than the beat root; their linkage is questionable and not used as a decisive control. The Konda correction reverses which comparison language appears to innovate.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 443 p.43 directly inspected; K03 Rule6 p.107 and Rule20 p.157

<a id="d444"></a>
## d444: pinch, pincers, tongs

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d444 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-uk-; distinct tool-name formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | u |
| Root/formation shape | VC-u-CC |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Velar verb/tool formation independently supported; labial Kui tool formation must be reconstructed separately. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | medium |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core-formation-uncertain |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil/Malayalam iṭukku and iṭukki independently support high u after ṭ. Kannada iḍaku provides a low-vowel variant, while Old Kannada iẓkuẓi has a different apical and internal structure.

**Direction.** Vowel-first southern pinch verbs favor earlier V–apical order, but the tool nouns do not all share an independently recoverable complete stem.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Tamil *iṭ-uk > iṭukku retains order. Kannada ikkuẓ and Tulu ikkuḷ may involve medial assimilation of the first apical, leaving another apical after k; alternatively their internal apical order reflects a different noun formation. Kui ḍīpa is an initial-displacement candidate, but i+u does not straightforwardly produce ī and its labial noun suffix differs.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** No Telugu attestation in this database group: record a gap, not a failure to change. Reconstructing *iṭi-pp solely to predict Kui ī would be circular. A source paradigm connecting the pinch verb to a labial noun, or an independently attested i-bearing formative, would distinguish contraction from another etymology. The superficial k/l reversal in tongs needs its own analysis, not the initial-metathesis label.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 444 p.43 directly checked

<a id="d445"></a>
## d445: narrow, crowded, abundant

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d445 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-u-k / *iṭ-ṭ-aḷ formation |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / geminate |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VCC-a-C (Telugu-matching strong formation) |
| Grammatical category | adjective/noun/verb |
| Boundary evidence | Gemination belongs to the independently matched ṭṭaḷ formation, not every derivative of the etymological root. |
| Input class | short-strong-or-mixed-structure |
| Telugu hypothesis | outside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | geminate-control |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭṭaḷam, Kannada iṭṭaḷa/iṭṭaṇa and Telugu iṭṭalamu independently support a geminate target in this formation, alongside a singleton high-u narrowness family iṭukku/iḍuku.

**Direction.** Both formations preserve initial i/e across southern languages; singleton and geminate stems must be classified separately before comparing Telugu.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭṭ-aḷ-am > Telugu iṭṭalamu with lateral simplification; crowded mass > abundant is independently bridged by Kannada meanings. The iṭ-uk narrowness words retain a singleton ṭ before a velar formative and cannot be treated as the identical input to iṭṭalamu.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Telugu is a geminate-formation control, not proof that its singleton *iṭuk input resisted metathesis: that input is not attested in Telugu here. Gadaba iḍigeda a few has different morphology and possible contact, while Badaga glade/nook and place names have queried etymologies. Broad connection with spatial d434/d448 or distress d435 is plausible but unproven.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 445 p.43; omitted nineteenth Tamil item source iṭakkar also checked

## d446: separate, distant

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d446 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-ay / *iṭ-av; regional *eṭ- |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-y / VC-a-v |
| Grammatical category | verb/adjective |
| Boundary evidence | ay and av formations independently visible; no unattested vowel distinction invented for davvu. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭai, Malayalam iṭayikka and Telugu eḍayu/eḍavu independently support vowel-first ordering with low second vowel; Malto eṛare provides a northern order comparison.

**Direction.** Retained southern and northern orders favor an earlier vowel-first root. Telugu davvu is likely related to eḍavu, but its a and geminate vv require more than simply exchanging the initial e and ḍ.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭ-ay > *eḍay > eḍayu regularly retains the initial vowel. A displacement analysis of davvu would require an earlier vowel or analogical variant, plus vv strengthening/shortening; *eḍ-av > *ḍēv does not directly yield davvu. Kolami davva/dautān and Naikri dʰāv may be Telugu-area loans, not independent support for the missing steps.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** K03 p.57 explicitly doubts the derivation of davvu/dhāv from *iṭ-a; his alternative discussion concerns voiced aspiration and a possible older laryngeal, not a demonstrated solution. Brahui is explicitly questioned in DEDR p.43. Nahali dhava is a contact-zone comparison, not a Dravidian cognate vote. The spatial-root relation to d434/d448 is a sensitivity hypothesis; do not silently explain the vowel by assuming different proto-roots.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 446 p.43 directly checked, including question mark before Brahui; K03 p.57 explicitly questions the etymology of davvu/dhāv

<a id="d447"></a>
## d447: grow weary, become thin

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d447 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-ay?; vowel reconstruction and lexical direction not final |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-ay |
| Grammatical category | verb |
| Boundary evidence | ay verbal base probable from Tamil; pp thirst noun is a separate morphological hypothesis, not a new positive. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | medium |
| Overall confidence | low |
| Eligibility / caveat | cognacy-or-input-uncertain |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭai weary is the sole independent unshifted witness in this entry. Telugu ḍayyu and Kuvi ḍah/daha/ḍāh agree semantically, but the imported initial *ḍaj reconstruction simply repeats the innovated-looking order.

**Direction.** Tamil vowel-first order, general apical correspondences, and Kuvi y/h comparison favor earlier *iṭay, provisionally; with only one unshifted branch, prothesis or imperfect cognacy cannot be ruled out on majority arithmetic.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *iṭay > an initial ḍay stem gives Telugu ḍayyu and Kuvi ḍah; the expected lowered/contracted ē and actual a are not reconciled. Kuvi length varies by source/lect. Kolami ḍay is explicitly a Telugu loan. Sastri 1969 p.111 derives Telugu dappi thirst from dayyu weary, offering an alternative to d109 aṭ-/aṇṭ- ancestry.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Do not invent an unattested *aṭay just to match a. The fatigue-to-thirst derivative is semantically and morphologically plausible (compare noccu/noppi in Sastri), but it needs historical attestation and comparison with southern thirst cognates before merging d109. It also must remain separate from homophonous destruction ḍappi d277.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 447 p.44; Sastri 1969 p.111, image verified (PDF136)

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭai, Malayalam iṭa/eṭa, Kannada eḍa/eḍe and Telugu eḍa/eḍamu independently agree on vowel-first spatial input; Kota eṛ supports the shortened noun.

**Direction.** The same independently supported order appears in place d434, whose forms and meanings overlap. Tulu dekkārɯ is a distinct compound/extension and does not reverse the reconstruction.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭay > *eḍay > eḍa; extended *iṭam > eḍamu. Tulu iḍɛ versus dekkārɯ may combine initial vowel loss with gemination and a leg-related compound component; exact segmentation requires a fuller dialect dictionary.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Merge with d434 in primary root counts. Toda dairy-vessel and Badaga ritual/toponym compounds do not add etyma. The Tulu initial-loss derivative remains ambiguous because its immediate full input is not attested here; no outcome-defined suffix class is proposed.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 448 p.44; primary family merged with 434

<a id="d449"></a>
## d449: left side

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d449 |
| Comparative input | *iṭ-a(y)/m; *eṭ- regional outcome |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | ṭ / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-C / VC-ay |
| Grammatical category | noun/adjective |
| Boundary evidence | a/m/ay left-side formations supported independently; short commands or clipping not assumed without source labels. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṭai/iṭam, Malayalam iṭam/eṭam, Kannada eḍa and Telugu eḍama support earlier vowel-first i/e plus retroflex. Kota/Toda and Kodagu agree in order, though vowel quality differs.

**Direction.** Telugu ḍā/dā is innovated relative to the comparative vowel-first left-side noun, but cannot be assigned the expected ē contraction without an additional vowel history. Tulu damma/datta has strengthening and local initial loss.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṭam > *eḍam > eḍama is retained. Aphaeresis/clipping of an already a-bearing derivative, analogy with regional left-side words, or displacement followed by vowel change may underlie ḍā/dā; the current source does not select one. Kolami edamakei is explicitly a Telugu loan and was mislabeled Telugu in the parsed corpus.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** DEDR separately assigns many other SCDr left words to Indo-Aryan *ḍavva/*ḍevva: Kui deba/debe/debo, Kuvi tebri, Gondi ḍema/demar/ḍāvā, etc. Those are a loan comparison, not absent cognates or shared metathesis. Source-only loan observations are inventoried separately. Naiki ḍākiyan kī may reflect regional borrowing; its full donor is unresolved.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 449 p.44; CDIAL 5539 loan comparison; source headings directly checked

**Independent input evidence.** Kolami Kinwat iṛp and Gondi Muria ḍīpi form the comparison. The database incorrectly assigns both to Kolami; source DEDR p.44 explicitly switches language.

**Direction.** Kolami vowel-first order and the regular possibility of retroflex-rhotic correspondence favor *iṬVp, but only one unshifted language is available; initial prothesis/loan history remains possible.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *iṭ-i-p > *ḍīp > Gondi ḍīpi would fit equal-vowel contraction, whereas Kolami iṛp could reflect medial syncope. However the missing formative i is not independently observed and must not be used as a deterministic prediction.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Treat Gondi as a probable but uncertain displacement case, not a dialectal Kolami D/R alternation. More wall nouns or a source derivational base could establish V2 and direction. No Telugu form is supplied; this is a comparative gap there.

**Direction.** Gondi order plus the recurring ṭ/ḍ correspondence supports a vowel-first regional input provisionally, but the common vowel and velar formative are not uniquely reconstructed.

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iṇai/iṇaŋku, Malayalam iṇa/iṇayuka, Kannada eṇe and Telugu ena/enayu support a retroflex nasal after an initial vowel, and low formative independently.

**Direction.** Agreement supports earlier iṇ-, with Telugu ṇ>n and southern lowering. Telugu nenayu retains a second n as well as an initial n, so it is not the result of simply moving the sole root nasal.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *iṇ-ay > *eṇay > enayu; derivative enucu/enupu has distinct palatal/labial morphology. nenayu can reflect added n through rebracketing or analogical reinforcement, but a source context is needed to choose. Tamil eḷḷu equal is explicitly questioned by DEDR and is not secure proof of a nasal/lateral root alternation.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** A control for the published exclusion of nasal C2. The initial n in nenayu cannot be counted as metathesis on surface inspection. The n survives medially, so deletion-plus-insertion or morphology would be required under a movement account. Comparison with iẓai d507 is tentative.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil ira/iravu, Malayalam iravu/irakkuka, Kannada era/eravu and Telugu eravu independently support i/e before r and a low formative.

**Direction.** The widespread vowel-first form, corroborated by Malto irɣre, favors original ir-; Tulu randuni is innovated under this comparison.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *ir-av > *erav > Telugu eravu preserves the order despite an input that could permit contraction. Tulu randuni may follow initial vowel loss in a nasal-bearing begging formation; its exact preceding full form is not attested here.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Do not explain Telugu retention by assigning an unsupported high formative: southern av words directly match its loan noun. Late lexical borrowing remains possible but is not documented, so this stays a genuine low-vowel retention counterexample. Tulu verbal morphology differs from eravu and does not prove a shared event.

<a id="d474"></a>
## d474: two

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d474 |
| Comparative input | *īr / *ir-V; nonhuman *ir-aṇ-ṭ; human *ir-u-var |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short-and-long-bound-allomorphs |
| C2 identity / structure | r / singleton |
| Following vowel | a/u |
| Root/formation shape | VC-V + gender/number formation |
| Grammatical category | numeral |
| Boundary evidence | Bound īr/iru, nonhuman aṇṭ and human u-var are independently motivated categories; comparisons/counts must not treat them as repeated independent etyma. |
| Input class | mixed-or-uncertain-quantity |
| Telugu hypothesis | outside narrow classical Telugu domain; no D prediction from that rule |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | high |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iru-/īr, Kannada iru/ir and eraḍu, Central Dravidian ir- forms and Brahui irā/iraṭ support vowel-first order independently. Nonhuman aṇṭ and human u-var formations can be distinguished by their morphology before their outcomes are inspected.

**Direction.** Wide independent retention of bound ir-/īr and the different human and nonhuman derivatives favors earlier ir-, not original r- with prothesis throughout the family. The shared r-initial nonhuman numeral across SCDr is strong comparative evidence, but recent Tamil/Malayalam/Tulu initial loss must be evaluated separately.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** K03 pp.159–160: *ir-aṇṭ > *eraṇḍ > hypothetical *rēṇḍ > Telugu reṇḍu with shortening before a nasal-stop cluster; other SCDr *ir-i/u-ṇṭ > *rīṇḍ with variable shortening and Konda backing to runḍi. Human *iru-var remains vowel-first in Telugu iruvuru and Gondi irvur; r+v assimilation yields Kannada/Old Telugu ibbar forms. Tamil/Malayalam/Tulu aphaeresis produces reṇṭu/raṇṭu/raḍḍɯ in later language histories. Malto *irw > iwr (corpus ivr) is a separate medial consonant transposition.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Do not count human, nonhuman, twenty, two hundred and ordinal derivatives as independent roots. Telugu retained iru/īr is a bound root and cannot be treated as an identical free-word input to reṇḍu. The short Telugu output does not prove that a long intermediate existed; *rēṇḍ is K03’s conditional reconstruction. Kui rīnḍe shows that pre-cluster shortening was not universal across languages. Konda iddum retains an initial vowel in a measure compound and needs separate cluster-assimilation/contact analysis. Kodagu daṇḍɨ, Markodi dad and Badaga ratte require local phonological/contact histories; do not automatically equate them with the SCDr innovation. Kurux ēṇḍ has a vowel history K03 explicitly calls puzzling. Toda ačok/acok is a measure term within an example, not another reflex of two.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 474 p.46 directly checked; K03 pp.159–160 and p.116; Hockings–Pilot-Raichoor 1992 pp.54,86,507; Canvin 2025 lect data

<a id="d475"></a>
## d475: jujube

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d475 |
| Comparative input | regional *ir-a-; nasal/velar and dental tree-name formations |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | r/l / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-NC / VC-a-C |
| Grammatical category | noun |
| Boundary evidence | Low vowel independently observed; exact dental/nasal/velar tree-name formatives are not assumed identical. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | medium |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil irati/irantai/ilantai, Malayalam ilanta and Kannada era/elaci support an initial vowel and medial liquid independently. The exact nasal-velar formation of Telugu rē̃gu is not matched by every southern tree name.

**Direction.** Independent retained southern forms favor earlier ir-/il- order. Original DEDR p.46 supplies actual Telugu rē̃gu/rēnu; the database instead mislabeled Kolami rēŋga as Telugu and omitted those Telugu forms.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *ir-aŋk > *eraŋk > *rēŋk > Telugu rē̃gu, with voicing/nasal developments; rēnu requires a different consonant change or variant. Tamil r/l alternation and dental rather than velar suffix need separate formation histories. Malayalam ilanta > lanta is straightforward initial vowel loss.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Kannada rēgu is explicitly borrowed from Telugu. Gondi, Kolami, Naikri/Naiki, Parji and Gadaba rēŋg-type tree names might spread with the plant name; no independent innovation is inferred just from initial r. More southern velar derivatives or historical recipient attestations would discriminate inheritance from diffusion. Malto ilkru has a different cluster. Source supplements do not add roots.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 475 p.46 directly checked; Southworth 2006 imported *irak is a proposal, not an attestation

## d476: deer, antelope

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d476 |
| Comparative input | *ir-al-ay, r/l order variation |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | r / singleton |
| Following vowel | a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-a-C-ay |
| Grammatical category | noun |
| Boundary evidence | Whole deer noun compared; later l/ḍ material in Telugu has no demonstrated identical formative ancestry. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | medium |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iralai and Kannada/Tulu eraḷe agree on initial vowel and r before later lateral; Malto ilaru has the liquids in the opposite order. Old Telugu iri also begins with a vowel.

**Direction.** The southern r...l agreement favors earlier *iral provisionally; Malto may show internal liquid reversal. Telugu lēḍi would require movement of a different liquid and an additional final consonant history, not just initial i/r metathesis.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Retained *iralay > eraḷe in Kannada/Tulu; reduced Old Telugu iri and strengthened iṟṟi require morphological/cluster changes. A proposed *ilara > *lēra > lēḍi path would need both an independent liquid reversal and a regular r/ḍ development; neither is established by this set.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** DEDR explicitly prefixes a question mark to Telugu lēṭi/lēḍi. Keep them uncertain rather than forcing them into a lateral-metathesis class. Malto internal reversal is separately plausible but not proved directionally by simple majority. Badaga iya may reflect liquid loss but is source-uncertain. Historical iri is the reliable Telugu retained comparison.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 476 p.46 directly checked, including question mark before lēṭi/lēḍi

| Initial consonant | Ø |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iraḷi/iṟali preserves an initial vowel plus two differently ordered-quality liquids. Kannada/Telugu rēla and Gondi rēlā share an r-initial plant name; only Tamil supplies the unshifted word here.

**Direction.** Earlier *iral- is plausible by the low-vowel contraction correspondence, but a Tamil prothetic adaptation of a regional rēl word remains possible without wider retained evidence.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *iral > *eral > *rēl > Telugu rēla-ceṭṭu; historical ṛēla gives an older r-initial attestation. Gondi rērkā requires an added velar and lateral/rhotic change; Kannada and Gondi may have borrowed the tree name.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Do not treat the imported *rēl as proved proto-input or Tamil as necessarily conservative. The old Telugu rhotic is transcribed ṛ in this source and should not be assigned a phonetic value without its inscriptional edition. Cassia is a Latin gloss incorrectly parsed as Telugu. Exact cognacy/donor history keeps this out of the decisive reconstructed-input cohort.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 477 p.46 directly checked

## d480: be, sit, abode

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d480 |
| Comparative input | *ir-u-; *ir-u-v / *ir-a-v place nouns |
| Initial consonant | Ø |
| V1 quality / quantity | i / short |
| C2 identity / structure | r / singleton |
| Following vowel | u/a |
| Root/formation shape | VC-u / VC-V-v / VC-C formations |
| Grammatical category | verb/noun |
| Boundary evidence | Existential high-u root and a/u place-noun formations distinguished; Kui suffix vowels not chosen from outputs. |
| Input class | short-vowel-initial-singleton-apical |
| Telugu hypothesis | eligible; obligatory application predicts D |
| Input confidence | high |
| Overall confidence | medium |
| Eligibility / caveat | core |

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iru/iruppu, Kannada iru/irdu and Kodagu ir- independently support a vowel-first existential root. Telugu iruvu/iravu retains noun formations; Malayalam irippu differs in formative vowel from Tamil iruppu.

**Direction.** The broad existential comparison favors earlier ir-. Kui rīnda/rīspa is innovative under its related steady/stand meaning, but its high-i length and added consonants require separate reconstruction.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Retained *iru-v > Telugu iruvu, with a-bearing iravu; Kannada irke > ikke and Telugu ikka are compatible with medial syncope plus assimilation. Tulu ippuni/itt- can continue r+labial/dental cluster assimilation. Kui *ir-i-nt/*ir-i-sp could yield rīnda/rīspa, but i in those exact formations is not independently established. Kota ig-/ir-/it- is a paradigm, not initial promotion.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Low-vowel Telugu iravu must not be erased by choosing only the high-u root label. Telugu iŋkuva has DEDR’s explicit alternative demonstrative iṅku d420. Kui rītka includes plural morphology and possible consonant-order changes, not another etymon. Badaga negative illa/ille is cross-linked but belongs to a separate negative-base analysis, not straightforward irregular sound change of iru.

**Mechanism scope.** Target initial-order comparison; literal exchange, assimilation and syncope distinguished in the derivation and language notes

**Scholarly references.** DEDR 480; DEN1 p.400 entry407; K03 existential reconstruction; alternative d420 for iŋkuva

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil iru great and irumai greatness provide the independent rhotic comparison; Telugu has inu- in compounds, especially inumikkili very great.

**Direction.** Tamil rhotic versus Telugu nasal can reflect assimilation before a following m in the compound. There is no evidence of r moving before the initial vowel.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Conditional *iru-mikkili > *inu-mikkili by anticipatory nasal influence, followed by extraction/generalization of inu- as a combining form. Compare Telugu inu māṟu twice (d474) and inumu iron (d486), without assuming all three have identical history.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Only a narrow two-language adjective comparison; no free Telugu inu paradigm is supplied, and the corpus inu is an in-construction fragment. Do not classify it as metathesis concealed by r loss unless an initial r-stage is independently attested. Compound-bound status is visible before outcome classification.

**Independent input evidence.** Malayalam iruviḷ/irūḷ, Kannada iruguṇḍi and Telugu iruguḍu/iruvuḍu support a vowel-first dark/tree component, tentatively compared with darkness d2552. Tamil īṭṭi and Tulu bīṭi differ too much to be the same simple input.

**Direction.** A retained ir-u formation is credible for part of the set. The b/v-initial wood names may reflect another tree word, compound reduction or contact, rather than relocation of r.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** Telugu iruguḍu/iruvuḍu retain ir-; ibbaḍa/ibbeḍa could reflect reduction/assimilation in a different compound or stem. Deriving bīṭi from iruguḍu by metathesis alone is impossible; additional consonant loss and formation differences are required.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Keep the complex plant-name family uncertain for inherited-law counts. The fact that blackwood can be named after darkness is a semantic hypothesis, not evidence for every segment. Tulu kari-bīṭi independently adds black, which can support either reinforcement or a different lexical base. No unsupported chain is selected.

**Independent input evidence.** Tamil irucu, Kannada irucu/iricu/iracu and Telugu irusu support vowel-first r plus a final coronal; second-vowel alternatives are independently attested.

**Derivation and relative chronology.** *ir-u-c > Telugu irusu is a possible coronal correspondence; Kannada ircu has medial syncope without initial movement. Gondi nirsu adds initial n and Kuvi hīrsū adds h/length after borrowing; these do not move r to word beginning.

**Exceptions and discriminating evidence.** Preserve a high-u control but flag the technical lexeme’s undated dissemination. Its possible wider loan origin should be researched before treating it as ancient inherited vocabulary. Kolami i·rcu is not explicitly marked a loan in this snippet, but its length and donor chronology remain uncertain. Parser Br/Early-Vedic tag on that form is not evidence of a Dravidian dialect.

## d485: mahua tree

| Property | Annotation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary family | d485 |
